subject: Distsamp: effects of det covariates change when covariates are added on abundance

messages.author: ea7d65e6eb7bf605
messages.subject: Distsamp: effects of det covariates change when covariates are added on abundance
parts:
I have used Unmarked for a couple different analyses, and I have always followed the same general procedure: 1) fit some models of detection with various combinations of covariates that might be important and choose the best one, then 2) fit some new models with various combinations of covariates on abundance/occupancy, using the best model selected in step 1) as the detection component.  However, I am currently using distsamp() and I'm finding that the best model in 1) is no longer the best fit once covariates are added in 2).  

Step 1)
lazb.10 <- distsamp(~1~tsb ,                   data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.11 <- distsamp(~tree~tsb ,                data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.12 <- distsamp(~shrub~tsb ,               data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.13 <- distsamp(~treeshrub~tsb ,           data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.14 <- distsamp(~tree+shrub~tsb ,          data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.15 <- distsamp(~tree+treeshrub~tsb ,      data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.16 <- distsamp(~tree+shrub+treeshrub~tsb, data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.17 <- distsamp(~BAsnag~tsb ,              data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")

According to lowest AIC, lazb.11 is the best model by far.  In fact, the covariate tree seems to have a very strong effect on detection probability.  So, naturally, I include the covariate "tree" in the detection component of all the models in step 2) below.

lazb.21 <- distsamp(~tree ~tsb + burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + elevation +fireID,                                           data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.22 <- distsamp(~tree ~tsb + burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + slope + elevation +fireID,                                   data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.23 <- distsamp(~tree ~tsb + burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb:burnsev + slope + elevation +fireID,                     data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.24 <- distsamp(~tree ~burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb + prefire + slope + elevation +fireID,                         data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.25 <- distsamp(~tree ~burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb + slope + aspect + elevation +fireID,                          data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.26 <- distsamp(~tree ~burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb + prefire + slope + aspect + elevation +fireID,                data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.27 <- distsamp(~tree ~burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb + tsb:burnsev + prefire + slope + aspect + elevation +fireID,  data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")
lazb.28 <- distsamp(~1    ~burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb + tsb:burnsev + prefire + slope + aspect + elevation +fireID,  data=umf.lazb, output="density", keyfun="hazard")

lazb.28 is exactly the same as lazb.27, except without the covariate "tree" on detection.  When I compare the AIC of all the models, lazb.28 is ranked higher than lazb.27, though only slightly.  So my questions are, why would the addition of covariates on abundance change the effects of covariates on detection?  Is there a better procedure for determining which is the best model?  

For context, the data comes from point count surveys of birds (in this case, Lazuli Bunting) and tree is an estimated tree cover. 

Any thoughts/suggestions welcome.  Thanks so much.

Paul

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Distsamp: effects of det covariates change when covariates are added on abundance
parts:
Hey Paul, this is not surprising.  Since detection is conditional on the latent state (e.g., abundance), when the expectation of that latent state changes due to covariates then you might find the detection function also changes a bit given that the data are fixed.

The approach to model selection that you used can be helpful for avoiding having to fit an unwieldy number of models, but it is not guaranteed to be adequate.  The paper that Richard cites in the help file for distsamp (Sillett et al. 2012 Ecological Applications) illustrates another approach to fitting multiple covariates without testing every single combination.  You'll also notice in their paper that the AIC rank of different model structures shifts around depending on which covariates are specified for each process.

The "best practices" for model selection vary depending on whom you ask.  :)
